title: Indian Green Card Holder Says He Wouldn't Move to US on an H-1B Today
excerpt: Mohamed Zeeshan, 32, self-petitioned for a green card from abroad and built a life in Virginia — but says the H-1B pathway has become too uncertain and unpredictable for today's immigrants.
body:
• Mohamed Zeeshan, a 32-year-old Indian national living in Arlington, Virginia, self-petitioned for a green card from abroad in 2021 and received it in 2023 — bypassing the H-1B system entirely.
  • Zeeshan says he was drawn to the US for its free speech protections and entrepreneurial culture, not purely for economic reasons.
  • He and his wife are delaying having children because her green card application is still pending, highlighting the ongoing uncertainty even for permanent residents.
  • Zeeshan says he would not come to the US on an H-1B visa today, citing employer dependency, the contested $100,000 fee, and rising denial rates for alternative visas.

Mohamed Zeeshan moved to the United States as a permanent resident in 2023. He runs his own consulting firm in Arlington, Virginia, and considers himself patriotic about American values. But in a first-person account published by Business Insider, the 32-year-old Indian national said he would not make the same move today if it required an H-1B visa.

"If I had to rely on an H-1B visa to come here today, I don't think I'd do it," Zeeshan said.

A Non-Linear Path to Permanent Residency

Zeeshan's route to the US did not follow the typical OPT-to-H-1B pipeline that most Indian graduates rely on. Born in Indonesia to Indian parents, he moved back to India at age 7 and later pursued a master's in international affairs at Columbia University, graduating in 2018.

After the 2016 election shifted rhetoric around immigration, Zeeshan said he felt employers were unwilling to sponsor international students. Rather than entering the H-1B lottery, he left the US for the Middle East, where he worked for a management consulting firm in Dubai.

"Instead of relying on the OPT-to-H-1B pathway, as many students do, I left the US and went to the Middle East," he said.

In 2021, he pursued an alternative: self-petitioning for a green card from abroad. He submitted extensive evidence showing his work was in the national interest, drawing on his background in research and public-interest issues. The green card was approved in 2023, freeing him from employer sponsorship entirely.

Drawn to American Values, Not Just Economics

Zeeshan said economic opportunity was not his primary motivation. He earned more in Dubai, where he paid no income tax, than in his first US job after receiving his green card.

"I was drawn to American ideals of free speech — the ability to write and speak freely about issues, even if they're controversial."

— Mohamed Zeeshan, author and consultant

As an Indian Muslim who has written a book about India as an emerging power, Zeeshan said the US offered a space to critique policymaking without backlash. He also cited the entrepreneurial culture with less bureaucratic regulation — he launched his own consulting firm in 2025.

His female friends from India, he added, have told him the US offers more freedom to build the careers and lives they want.

The H-1B System's Growing Uncertainty

Despite his own secure status, Zeeshan said the H-1B pathway has become increasingly fraught. The visa ties workers to a single employer who can terminate them at any time, and losing that job triggers a 60-day scramble to find new sponsorship or leave the country.

Recent policy changes have compounded the uncertainty. The Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B fee — imposed in September 2025 and later struck down by a federal judge as an unlawful tax, though the ruling remains tied up in appeals — rattled both employers and workers. The wage-weighted selection system that replaced the random lottery has reshaped who gets selected.

"The H-1B temporary work visa was already an uncertain and inefficient route when I was graduating," Zeeshan said. "Your visa is tied to an employer who can fire you at any time, and losing your job makes you vulnerable to having to leave the country. You're always on edge."

Family Life on Hold

Even with a green card, Zeeshan's family faces immigration-related constraints. He and his wife rent an apartment in Arlington, but they are delaying having children because her green card application is still pending.

"We want to minimize uncertainty about her situation before having kids," he said. Their decision, unconventional by Indian cultural standards where couples are expected to have children soon after marriage, reflects the long tail of immigration uncertainty that extends beyond any single visa category.

Looking at Other Options

Zeeshan said he tries to inform others about pathways beyond the H-1B, such as the EB-1A visa for individuals with "extraordinary" ability. But even these alternatives are becoming harder — data shows EB-1A denial rates are increasing.

He noted that relatives and friends are now looking at Germany, Australia, and other countries because landing a job and a visa in the US after graduating has become so difficult.

"I intend to naturalize and become a US citizen, unless something makes that difficult," Zeeshan said. "We can't say what rule changes might happen."
nri_angle: Zeeshan's story captures a growing sentiment among Indian immigrants who value American freedoms but see the H-1B system as an increasingly risky bet, with many now exploring alternative pathways or other countries entirely.
author: Diaspora Desk
